peter, below is the most recent exchange i was referring to. yes, the situation is slightly different (bipartite/multiple networks instead of unipartite) but the second solution is still relevant. that is, what i would do if i were you is to create a new (second) network consisting only of ties that are NOT permitted in the first network; create a model in which this second network is used as an edge covariate to explain the first network; and then use the offset() function to fix that parameter at -Inf, effectively forbidding those ties from being created.

i hope this helps. best wishes,

-kevin



hi christian,



i had a related earlier question on this too, and so can pass along the advice i received from steve and pavel. i'll caution, however, that while this indeed provided me with a solution for my problem that makes intuitive sense to me (and seems to directly parallel the "structural zeroes" situation in Siena), there may be other reasons for which this fix is undesirable/inappropriate, especially for the case of multiple networks? so i will still be curious to hear if others have further thoughts.



basically you can do exactly what you suggest- create a joint adjacency matrix of all networks- and then i'm aware of two possible ways to prohibit ties "between" networks:



1) more straightforward: create a node attribute that has a different value for membership in each of the different networks; include a "nodemix" term in your model, and use the "base" argument to only include those effects from the mixing matrix that correspond to ties ACROSS networks; and fix those parameters at -Inf (i have had mixed experience with this in the past... sometimes you may not have to fix the parameter because ergm will recognize that no ties are present and do this for you automatically... sometimes it does not and so you have to do this manually using offset, see below).



2) more cumbersome: basically the same thing, but do this using an edge covariate instead of a node covariate. in other words, create a matrix where values for ALL ties WITHIN networks are set to zero, and ALL ties ACROSS networks are set to one, feed this into your model using an edgecov term, and again fix that effect at -Inf using the offset() function, e.g. offset(edgecov(X)).



i hope this is helpful... but others please let us know if for some reason this approach is problematic! or if there is an easier approach i'm unaware of. best wishes,



-kevin

Hi, Alex.  Here's some code that you can use in R.  I haven't checked it thoroughly, but I think it works?

First, I saved your excel spreadsheet as a .csv file after deleting what appeared to be a bunch of extraneous commas in some of the entries.  The csv is attached.  After saving it in the R working directory, try:

blog <- read.csv("bloggers.csv")
f <- function(a) as.numeric(names(blog) %in% a) # returns a 43-vector of zeros and ones, where 1 means the corresponding blogger is on the list 'a'.
y <- sapply(blog, f) # create 43-by-43 matrix of directed relationships, where y[i,j] = 1 if and only if i is on j's list.

rownames(y) <- names(blog) # Add names to rows of y for ease of reading
y[1:5, 1:5] # check out a subnetwork

z <- outer(1:43, 1:43, Vectorize(function(a, b) sum(y[,a]*y[,b]==1))) # Now use the "outer" idea in your code below to give the final matrix.
rownames(z) <- colnames(z) <- names(blog)
z[1:5, 1:5] # Check out a bit of the final answer.  Notice that the diagonal gives the total number of friends for each blogger.


By the way, the logic of the R code you were given isn't quite correct, since it counts not only common friends but also common non-friends.

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] problem in fitting STERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Olivier,

I've spent some time delving into this.  I don't see any obvious bugs 
anywhere, in either your code or in ours.  Instead, I think it is mostly 
related to an issue with fitting stergms that we've identified and have 
some resolution on already.  The basic issue comes from the fact that in 
networks with relatively low density and relatively long relational 
duration, there are very few ties changing from one time step to the 
next.  This makes it very difficult to conduct STERGM estimation, since 
much of the information it needs to work with is embedded in the 
relational changes between time steps.

Nicole Carnegie and some of us have a paper that we've just submitted 
that explores this issue, and develops an approximation that works best 
precisely when the problem is greatest.  It allows one to obtain a good 
estimate for the STERGM parameters without even having to run the STERGM 
fitting. We also work through an example of it in the STERGM tutorial 
that we did at this past Sunbelt, so that may be the place to start to 
learn about it at the moment. See Section 9 of:

http://csde.washington.edu/statnet/Resources/Sunbelt2012/STERGM/STERGMtutorial.pdf

If your goal in fitting the model is primarily to drive a simulation, 
this may really be all that you need.  Take a look, and let us know if 
this helps or not, and if you need any more advice.

Cheers,
Steve

Dear Olivier,

I've run your example, and I think that part of the problem is that you
are controlling the degree distribution too rigidly.

You have a network with 1600 nodes and 800 edges (on average), (i.e.,
mean degree of 1, for this undirected network).

However, you specify that 176 nodes (on average) must be isolates and
1394 must have degree 1. This leaves only 30 nodes (on average) with
unspecified degree. The mean degree is then

(176*0 + 1394*1 + 30*x)/1600,

where x is the mean degree of the remaining 30 nodes. To get an overall
mean degree of 1 (implied by the edge count), x has to be 6.87. That is,
an average of 11% of the nodes should be isolates, an average of 87%
should have degree 1, and the remaining 2% should somehow have an
average degree of 6.87.

What this means in practice is that the distribution of networks that
fulfills this constraint is almost certainly going to be weird, probably
bimodal. Finding the parameters to induce that distribution --- if they
exist --- is going to be very difficult regardless of algorithm, and you
probably don't want this model and targets for your simulation anyway.

                          I hope this helps,
                          Pavel

Hi, Olivier,

> The dynamic network on which I am actualy working on is very close to
> the one I have sent to the mailing list. The number of edges is a bit
> lower (mean number of edges=0.92)

That turns out to make a pretty big difference, since it means that
those remaining 30 actors would only need to have mean degree of 2.6,
which is more likely to be doable, though it might be hard to get just
the right configuration, especially since the dissolution process isn't
very "respectful" of degree distribution.

> I have actually found 'manually' parameters that fit to my data. I
> have simulated a 100 of list of dynamic network using these parameters
> and it seems to be close to what I expect (cross sectionnal network
> statistics are close to the targets and the number of deleted and
> added edges also).
> Please find attach the network of 10000 edges and the dynamic
> parameters.
> 2 questions:
> 1) is it possible to find the parameters of this dynamic network using
> stergm or the constraints are still to rigid?

As I said above, it might still be possible, though with difficulty. One
possibility might be to instead use edges + isolates + concurrency (#
actors with degree 2 or greater), and see what you get. (There are
reasons to believe that it might have an easier time fitting that,
because concurrency always increases in the number of edges, whereas
number of actors with degree 1 increases, up to a point, then
decreases.)

> 2) if it is not possible, why is it possible to find reasonable
> parameters manually?

Yes, but with a lot of trial and error.

                             Pavel

Ya,

It is because we are trying to simulate a network that "looks like" the 
one our data are collected from.  For us, specifically, this is because we 
want to explore the dynamic implications of network structure for 
diffusion (we're working on HIV transmission analyses).

Network terms tend to be much more highly correlated than terms in GLMs 
for independent data.  So if we wanted to simulate "realistic 
networks", it is not trivial to find the parameter values that 
reproduce observed network statistics.  Estimation allows us to find the 
parameter estimates that reproduce these statistics -- for models that 
include statistics that can be observed in the data.

best, Martina

Ya,

Dynamic simulations are appropriate if the research question you have 
concerns dynamic properties of network processes (like diffusion).

You can also use simulations for static networks to assess either goodness 
of fit (see the paper by Hunter and Goodreau 2008 at 
http://pubs.amstat.org/doi/pdf/10.1198/016214507000000446) or assess the 
range of variation of the networks described by the fitted model.

Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] simulate a large network
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet community,

I got the following error when simulating networks with 1500 or more nodes.

Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
 Too many unique dyads!

I used this piece of code to produce the ergm stats for the simulate().
Nodal attributes attr1 and attr2 are asked to match high homophily
specified in meanstats. I read an old thread on the statnet help archive
about this error and I used the tip by David Hunter to set maxNumDyadTypes
as a very big number, e.g. 1e+20 and still got this error. Is there a way
that it can be fixed so that ergm allows to simulate a larger size network?
It worked for a network with 1000 nodes (without using the control option)
.

ergm1 <- ergm(net~ density+absdiff('attr1')+absdiff('attr2'), burnin=1e+6
, meanstats=c(0.008, 500,500),
 control=control.ergm(maxNumDyadTypes=big.enough))

Thanks in advance!

Best,
Yongren Shi
